title: What generative AI is and is not
summary: A plain, accurate explanation of what generative AI actually is, how it works, and the common myths that get businesses into trouble.

evidence: Primary technical documentation from model providers
Representative model outputs and failure cases
Current professional guidance where consequential uses are discussed
methodology: Define generative AI by what the model does
Separate pattern generation from knowledge and judgment
Compare suitable and unsuitable tasks
Test claims against observable outputs

editorialIntro: An honest mental model of generative AI, so you know what the tool actually does before you spend money or trust its output.

blocks.text: Generative AI is software that produces new text, images, audio, or code by predicting what comes next from patterns it learned across very large amounts of example data. The systems most businesses touch are large language models (LLMs) like the ones behind ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. You give the model a prompt, and it returns a response one token at a time. Each token is chosen because it is a statistically likely continuation of everything that came before.

A useful way to hold this in your head: an LLM is a very well-read pattern completer. It has read a wide slice of the public internet, books, and documents, and it has become good at continuing text so it sounds right. That single fact explains both its strengths (fluent drafting, summarizing, reformatting, brainstorming) and its failures (confident wrong answers, invented sources, shaky arithmetic).

It is not a database you query for stored facts, and it does not check its work against the world. It is a prediction machine that is often correct because correct-sounding text and correct text overlap a lot, but not always.

This lesson is for owners, operators, and team leads who are being asked to "use AI" and want a foundation they can trust before they build anything on top of it. You do not need a technical background. If you can describe a task to a new hire in plain language, you have the skill that matters most here.

items: A small-business owner deciding whether AI belongs in customer service, marketing, or operations.
A manager writing a policy for how the team may and may not use these tools.
Anyone who has heard both "AI will replace everyone" and "AI is useless" and wants a grounded middle view.

editorialSections.title: When to use it, and when not

blocks.text: When to use it

Read this before your first serious project, before you sign up for a paid plan, and before you let AI touch anything a customer or regulator will see. This mental model is the thing that keeps you out of trouble later. Come back to it whenever a vendor makes a claim that sounds too good, because most overclaims collapse the moment you remember the model is predicting text rather than knowing facts.
When not to use it

Do not reach for generative AI as your source of truth for anything with a real-world answer you can look up: a specific law, a dosage, a tax figure, a customer's account balance, a quote you plan to attribute to a real person. The model will happily produce all of these, and it will sometimes be wrong in ways that look completely convincing. When the cost of being wrong is high and the fact is checkable, check the source, not the chatbot.
To build the mental model, spend time in the four consumer chat tools most businesses start with. Each has a free tier that is enough to learn on.
ChatGPT
Seeing the broadest range of tasks, with strong general drafting. Free tier available.
Claude
Longer documents, careful writing, and following detailed instructions. Free tier available.
Gemini
Working inside Google Docs, Gmail, and Search. Free tier available.
Perplexity
Watching how a tool cites sources, with answers that include links you can click. Free tier available.

A good exercise: ask all four the same factual question, then check every answer against a primary source. You will learn more about how these systems behave in twenty minutes of that than in an hour of reading.
Use this to build an accurate feel for the technology.

items: Give it a drafting task. Ask a model to write a short thank-you email to a customer. Notice how fluent and fast it is. This is the core strength.
Give it a lookup task. Ask for a specific statistic or a citation, then verify it. Notice whether the source is real.

Push on a wrong answer. When it gets something wrong, tell it so. Watch how it apologizes and often produces a new answer that also sounds confident. This shows you the model has no independent access to truth.
Ask it to do arithmetic in its head. Try a multi-step calculation, then try again with a tool or calculator enabled. Compare.
Write down your own one-sentence definition. After the exercises, describe what the tool is in your own words. That sentence is the asset you keep.

blocks.text: Copy these into any chat tool to feel the difference between generation and knowledge.
Write a warm, three-sentence follow-up email to a customer named Dana who just bought a kayak from our shop. Do not invent any details about the order.

I'm testing you. Give me the full citation for a peer-reviewed study showing that four-day work weeks raise productivity. Then, separately, tell me your confidence that this exact study exists and can be found by that citation.
Here is a paragraph I wrote. Rewrite it to be clearer and shorter, but do not add any facts I did not include. Flag anything you were tempted to add.
The email prompt returns something usable in seconds:

"Hi Dana, thank you so much for picking up your kayak from us today. We hope it brings you a lot of calm mornings on the water. If anything ever needs adjusting, just reach out and we'll take care of it."
The citation prompt is where the lesson lands. A well-behaved model will often say something like:

"I can describe the general finding, but I should be honest: I may not be able to give you an accurate, verifiable citation. Any specific author, journal, and year I produce should be checked against a database like Google Scholar before you rely on it. My confidence that a precise citation I generate is real and correct is low."
That second output is the whole point. The tool is useful and it is also fallible, and a good one will tell you which is which.
Treating fluency as accuracy
The most common error. Smooth, confident prose feels true. It is not evidence of truth.
Assuming it "knows" your business
Out of the box, the model knows nothing about your customers, prices, or policies. It fills gaps with plausible invention unless you supply the facts.
Believing the training data is current
Models have a knowledge cutoff and may not know recent events unless connected to live search. Even then, verify.
Thinking a bigger model means always right
More capable models are wrong less often, not never. The verification habit still applies.
Pasting sensitive data without checking policy
Consumer tiers may use your inputs to improve models unless you opt out or use a business plan. Know your settings before sharing anything private.

items: ✓ Did I ask the model to do something it is good at (generate, reshape, summarize) rather than something it cannot reliably do (recall exact facts, do precise math)?
✓ Have I verified every factual claim, name, number, and citation against a primary source?
✓ Did I supply the real facts about my business rather than let the model guess?
✓ Is anything customer-facing, legal, medical, or financial getting a human sign-off?
✓ Do I know whether my inputs are being used to train the model, and am I comfortable with that?

title: What AI can and cannot do for business
summary: A concrete, honest map of the business tasks generative AI does well, the ones it does badly, and how to tell them apart before you invest.
audience: Leaders and operators deciding where AI belongs in real business workflows.
methodology: Describe the task before selecting a tool
Separate drafting and classification from authority and judgment
Score reversibility and consequence
Run a representative test
Assign human review before adoption

The organization can identify consequential decisions
limitations: Performance varies by model, data, and task
Task suitability does not establish privacy, security, or regulatory acceptability
editorialIntro: The fastest way to waste money on AI is to aim it at the wrong job. This lesson gives you a working map: the task shapes AI handles well, the ones it botches, and a simple test for telling them apart before you commit.

blocks.text: This is a practical taxonomy of business work, sorted by how well current generative AI performs it. The dividing line is not "hard versus easy" the way a person would judge it. It is "does this task reward fluent pattern completion, or does it require verified truth, live data, precise math, or accountability?"

AI is strong when the task is to produce a draft, reshape existing information, or generate options. It is weak when the task is to be the authoritative source of a fact, to act on real-time private data it has not been given, or to make a judgment that someone must answer for. The rest of this lesson turns that principle into a checklist you can apply to any request that lands on your desk.

The one-line test: if a smart, fast intern could draft it from information you hand them, and you would still review it, AI can probably help. If the task needs a guaranteed-correct fact, a live system lookup, or a signature, AI is a starting point at most.

editorialSections.title: Who this is for and when to use it

items: Owners and operators deciding where to pilot AI first.
Team leads triaging a backlog of "can AI do this?" requests.
Anyone building a business case and needing a sober view of the payoff.

blocks.text: You do not need to know how the models work. You do need to know your own workflows well enough to describe them.

Use this map when you are choosing a first project, when a vendor pitches an "AI solution" and you want to sanity-check it, and when you are writing the rules for how your team may use these tools. Start where the task is high-volume, low-stakes, and easy to review. That is where AI pays off fastest and where a mistake costs the least while you learn.
Avoid AI as the decision-maker or the final word in these situations:

items: Anything where a wrong answer causes real harm and cannot be caught in review: dosing, safety instructions, structural or financial calculations people act on directly.

Authoritative facts about your own operations that the model has no access to: account balances, order status, inventory, who owes what. Connect a real system for those; do not ask the model to guess.
Legal, medical, and financial advice presented as reliable. AI can help you prepare questions for a professional. It is not the professional.
Situations demanding accountability. When someone must be answerable for a decision, a human makes it. The model cannot be held responsible.

blocks.text: First drafts
Marketing copy, emails, job posts. Reach for ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini.
Summarizing long documents and meetings
Claude handles long docs well; Gemini works inside Google apps.
Answering with cited web sources
Perplexity, or the search modes in ChatGPT and Gemini.
Reformatting data, drafting spreadsheets and code
ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. Always run and check what they produce.
Customer answers from your knowledge base
Use a retrieval-based assistant grounded in your own docs, not raw chat.
Exact math, live account data, legal rulings
Use connected tools, databases, and professionals for these.

items: List the task in plain words. Write what a person would actually do, start to finish.
Sort each step into generate/reshape (AI-friendly) or verify/decide/lookup (human or connected system).
Score the stakes. If it is wrong, who notices, how fast, and how bad is it? Low-stakes and reviewable goes first.
Check the data. Does AI need facts it does not have? Either give it those facts in the prompt or connect a real source.
Design the review step before you launch. Decide who checks output and against what.
Pilot small, measure, then scale only the steps that saved real time without adding risk.

blocks.text: Here are my last five approved customer replies (pasted below). Draft a reply to this new message in the same tone. Only use facts from the message and my notes. If you need information I didn't give you, list your questions instead of guessing.

Summarize this 12-page vendor contract into a one-page brief for a non-lawyer: key dates, payment terms, termination, and anything unusual. Quote the exact clause for each point so I can verify it. Flag anything you're unsure about.
I run a landscaping company. Draft three social posts about our spring cleanup service. Do not invent prices, dates, or promotions. Leave a [bracket] anywhere I need to fill in a real detail.
The contract prompt returns a brief that is genuinely useful because it quotes the source:

Payment terms: Net 30 from invoice date. Clause 4.2: "Payment shall be due within thirty (30) days of receipt of a valid invoice." Unusual: an auto-renewal with a 90-day cancellation window. Clause 9.1. This is longer than typical; confirm you can meet it. I am not certain this is enforceable in your state, so treat it as a flag for a lawyer, not advice.
The landscaping prompt returns posts with honest gaps left for you:
"Spring is here and so is the mess winter left behind. Book your spring cleanup with us and get your yard ready for the season. [Add your offer or start date here.] Call [phone] to reserve a slot."
Aiming AI at a lookup problem
"What's this customer's balance?" is a database question, not a chat question. The model will guess.
Skipping the review step to save time
The review is where the value gets protected. Cutting it turns a time-saver into a liability.
Piloting on your highest-stakes work
Learn on the low-risk tasks first, where a caught error is cheap.
Believing vendor claims without a test
Ask to see the tool fail. One that cannot show you its limits is hiding them.
Grounding a customer bot in the open model instead of your own documents
Ungrounded, it will invent policies you do not have.

items: ✓ Is this a generate/reshape task, or does it secretly need a verified fact or live data?
✓ Did I supply the real information, or is the model filling gaps by inventing?
✓ Are the stakes low enough that a caught error is cheap, or do I need tighter controls?
✓ Is there a named human reviewing anything customer-facing or high-stakes?
✓ For legal, medical, or financial content, is a qualified professional in the loop?

title: When not to use AI

editorialIntro: Knowing where a model does not belong is what separates people who use AI well from people who get burned by it. This lesson draws the honest boundaries.

editorialSections.title: The moments to close the chat window

blocks.text: A clear list of the situations where the right move is to stop and hand off to a person.

AI is a strong drafting and thinking partner, useful across a wide range of work. But it predicts plausible text. It does not know what is true, it does not carry responsibility, and it does not understand the stakes of your specific situation. This lesson names the categories where those limits turn from harmless into dangerous.
The goal is not to make you afraid of the tool. It is to give you a short set of tripwires, so you can use AI aggressively everywhere else, knowing you have marked off the places it should not go.

items: Business owners and teams who have started using AI and now need to know where to stop.
Anyone tempted to ask a chatbot a question whose wrong answer could cost real money, health, or legal standing.
Managers writing an AI policy who want the "do not" list to be concrete instead of a vague warning.

editorialSections.title: Four features that should make you slow down

blocks.text: Pull up these boundaries whenever a task has one of these features: a decision you cannot easily reverse, a fact you cannot check, a person who could be harmed by an error, or a rule you are legally bound to follow. If any are present, read the next section carefully.

editorialSections.title: When not to use AI — specific boundaries

blocks.text: The reliable test: could a confident, wrong answer hurt someone or expose you? If yes, AI is a research assistant at most, and a qualified human owns the decision.
High-stakes legal, medical, and financial decisions

Do not treat a model's output as legal, medical, or financial advice. It can explain concepts and help you prepare questions for a professional. It cannot account for your jurisdiction, your full history, current regulation, or the cost of being wrong. A confident paragraph about your tax situation, a medication interaction, or a contract clause is a starting point for a conversation with a qualified human, never the final word. Nothing on this site is legal, medical, or financial advice, and RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney.
Facts you cannot verify

If the model states a statistic, a case citation, a quote, a date, or a source and you have no way to check it, do not use it. Models produce fluent, confident text that is sometimes simply wrong, and the fabricated version looks identical to the real one. Invented legal citations have already gotten lawyers sanctioned. If verification is impossible, the output is not usable.
Confidential or regulated data

Do not paste client records, patient details, trade secrets, unreleased financials, or anything covered by a confidentiality agreement into a tool that is not contractually cleared for it. See the Privacy and Confidentiality lesson for the full breakdown.
Genuine human-judgment calls

Firing someone, resolving a conflict between two people, deciding whether to trust a partner, comforting someone in crisis, making an ethical call where reasonable people disagree: these need a human who carries the weight of the outcome. A model can help you think through options, but the choice, and the accountability, stay with you.
Anything you could not defend

If a regulator, a client, or a court asked "why did you say this," and your only answer is "the AI wrote it," you should not ship it. Ownership of the work has to sit with a person who understands it and can stand behind it.

editorialSections.title: Tools for the safe version of these tasks

blocks.text: When a task sits near a boundary, the fix is often to change what you ask for, not to abandon AI entirely.

items: Perplexity, or a model with browsing and citations: better when you need sources you can click and verify, rather than an unsourced claim.
Claude and ChatGPT: strong for drafting the list of questions to bring to your lawyer, doctor, or accountant, so you arrive prepared rather than relying on the model's answer.
Your professional's own portal, or a human specialist: for the actual decision. No general model replaces this.

blocks.text: Use AI to prepare for the expert conversation. Do not use it to skip the expert.

editorialSections.title: The boundary check, step by step

items: Name the task in one sentence. Vague tasks hide their stakes.
Ask: is this reversible? If undoing a mistake is hard or impossible, raise your caution level.
Ask: can I verify the output? If not, it is not usable as fact.
Ask: could a wrong answer harm a person or expose me legally? If yes, a qualified human owns the decision.
Ask: is confidential or regulated data involved? If yes, apply the privacy rule before anything else.
Decide the role. Full draft, research assistant only, or hands off entirely. Write down which one.

blocks.text: These keep AI in a safe, boundary-respecting role.

I have a meeting with my [accountant / attorney / doctor] about [topic]. Do not give me advice or tell me what to do. Instead, write a list of smart questions I should ask so I understand my options and risks. Flag anything where the answer depends on my specific situation.
I'm about to rely on the claim below. List every specific fact, number, citation, or source in it that I would need to independently verify before trusting it. Mark which ones you cannot confirm.
Help me think through a difficult people decision. Lay out the possible approaches, the tradeoffs of each, and questions I should sit with. Do not decide for me; I own the outcome.

editorialSections.title: What a good response looks like

blocks.text: From the verification prompt, a strong response reads like this:
Claims to verify before you rely on this:

items: "The deadline is 30 days" — I cannot confirm the current rule for your jurisdiction. Check the governing agency's site or ask a professional.
"Studies show a 40% improvement" — no source given; treat as unverified until you find the primary study.
The cited case name — I may have this wrong or invented it. Confirm it exists in an official reporter before citing it anywhere.

blocks.text: A weaker model answers with breezy confidence and no caveats. That contrast is the whole point: the useful output is the one that helps you check, not the one that sounds sure.
Treating fluent as correct
Confidence in the writing tells you nothing about accuracy.
Using AI advice to skip a professional
The model does not carry the liability. You do.
Citing what you did not verify
Fabricated citations have real, documented consequences.
Letting convenience override the boundary
The riskiest moment is when you are busy and the shortcut is tempting.
Assuming a newer, bigger model removed these limits
It reduced some errors. It did not make the model accountable or all-knowing.

items: This decision is reversible, or I have accepted the risk of it not being.
Every fact I am relying on has been verified at a real source.
No high-stakes legal, medical, or financial call is being made on the model's say-so.
A qualified human owns any decision that could harm a person or expose the business.
No confidential or regulated data went anywhere it should not.
I can explain and defend this output without saying "the AI wrote it."

title: Prompting fundamentals
summary: The practical technique behind useful AI prompts: context, examples, constraints, structure, and iteration, grounded in provider guidance.
audience: People who want more consistent, inspectable output from general-purpose AI assistants.
methodology: State the task and intended user
Supply relevant context and examples
Specify boundaries and output structure
Ask for uncertainty to be exposed
Evaluate and revise against the real task
assumptions: The user can provide enough context to define the task
Prompting is one layer of a governed workflow
limitations: A stronger prompt cannot repair missing evidence or unsuitable model use
Prompting does not guarantee factual accuracy, privacy, or compliance
editorialIntro: Most bad AI output comes from thin prompts, not weak models. Learn the five moves that reliably raise quality: role, context, examples, structure, and iteration.

blocks.text: A prompt is the instruction you give an AI model. Good prompting is the skill of describing a task so clearly that a capable but literal assistant, one with no memory of your world, produces what you actually wanted on the first or second try. The published guidance from the major labs converges on a small set of techniques. This lesson covers the ones that pay off for everyday business work.

The core idea: the model cannot read your mind, and it will not ask for missing details unless you invite it to. Everything you leave unsaid, it either omits or invents. Good prompting is mostly the discipline of saying the unsaid things.
The five moves

cells.text: Tells the model the perspective to write from ("You are a careful bookkeeper explaining to a first-time owner").
Supplies the facts it needs: your audience, your constraints, the source material.
Shows one or two samples of the output you want. Often the single highest-leverage move.
Specifies format, length, and sections. Use clear delimiters to separate instructions from data.
Treats the first output as a draft and refines with specific feedback.

editorialSections.title: Who this is for and when to use it

blocks.text: Who this is for

items: Anyone whose AI results feel generic, off-tone, or wrong, and who suspects the problem is the prompt.
Team members who write prompts other people rely on and want a repeatable method.
Owners building templates so the whole team gets consistent output.

blocks.text: When to use it

Use these techniques on any task you will repeat, any output that must match a specific tone or format, and any request where a vague prompt already gave you a disappointing result. The payoff scales with repetition: a well-built prompt you reuse fifty times is worth the ten minutes it takes to write carefully.
When not to use it

For a quick one-off ("what's a synonym for reliable?"), an elaborate prompt is wasted effort. Just ask. And no amount of prompting fixes a task the model fundamentally cannot do. If the job requires a guaranteed-correct fact the model does not have, or precise math, better wording will not make an invented answer true. Prompting improves how well the model does what it can do. It does not extend what it can do.
These techniques transfer across every major assistant: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity. Two practical notes.

First, Claude and ChatGPT both respond well to clear structure and delimiters, and both vendors publish prompt guides worth reading (Anthropic's prompt engineering documentation and OpenAI's prompting guidance). Second, "Projects" or "custom instructions" features let you store role and context once so you do not repeat them every message. Use them for anything recurring.

items: State the role and goal in one line. Who is the model being, and what is the single outcome?
Paste the context and source material, clearly separated. Use a label like SOURCE: or triple quotes so the model knows what is data versus instruction.
Add one or two examples of the output you want, if you have them. This anchors tone and format better than description alone.
Specify structure: format, length, sections, and what to leave out.
Invite honesty: tell it to ask questions or flag uncertainty rather than guess.
Read the output as a draft. Give specific feedback ("tighten the second paragraph; the tone is too formal") and run again.
Save the winner as a reusable template with [brackets] for the parts that change.

blocks.text: A thin prompt versus a built one, same task.
Thin: "Write a cancellation email."
Built:

ROLE: You are a warm but professional customer-service lead for a small yoga studio. TASK: Write an email to a member who is canceling their membership. Goal: keep the door open without pressure. CONTEXT: Member's name is Priya. She's been with us 14 months. No complaint on record; she mentioned moving. Our policy: cancellation takes effect at the end of the current billing cycle. We offer a "pause" option for up to 3 months. FORMAT: Under 130 words. No discount offers. Mention the pause option once, gently. End with a genuine thank-you. If you're missing any fact you need, ask me instead of inventing it.
A structure-and-delimiter example for working over source text:
Rewrite the SOURCE below as three bullet points a busy owner can scan. Keep every number exactly as written. Do not add claims. SOURCE: """ [paste the raw text here] """
The thin prompt returns a generic template full of blanks and a tone that could belong to any company. The built prompt returns something close to send-ready:

"Hi Priya, thank you for letting us know, and for the fourteen months you spent practicing with us. Your cancellation will take effect at the end of your current billing cycle, so nothing changes before then. If your move turns out to be temporary, we can pause your membership for up to three months instead, whenever you like. Either way, you're always welcome back on the mat. Wishing you a smooth move. Warmly, The Studio Team"
The difference is not a smarter model. It is a prompt that supplied the role, the facts, the format, and permission to ask rather than guess.
Leaving out the facts and hoping
Unstated details get invented. Supply them.
Mixing instructions and data
Without delimiters, the model may treat your source text as a command. Separate them clearly.
Over-stuffing one prompt
Ten competing instructions produce mush. Prioritize, then iterate for the rest.
Prompting a factual claim into existence
Asking confidently does not make an answer true. Verify facts regardless of prompt quality.
Not saving what works
A great prompt you retype from memory each time is a great prompt you will slowly ruin. Template it.

items: Did I give a role, the real context, and a clear format?
Are instructions and source data separated so the model can tell them apart?
Did I include an example when tone or format matters?
Did I invite the model to ask questions or flag uncertainty instead of guessing?
Did I still verify every fact in the output, since good prompting does not guarantee truth?
Did I save the working prompt as a reusable template?

title: Hallucinations and risk
summary: What AI hallucinations are, why they happen, the real consequences of fabricated output, and the controls that reduce or expose them.
audience: Researchers, writers, professionals, and teams relying on factual or cited AI output.
evidence: Primary court and professional records for documented failures
methodology: Identify claims that require authority
Require source-level evidence
Separate fluent wording from factual support
Test citations and quotations directly
Escalate unresolved claims before publication
assumptions: Users have access to authoritative sources
Consequential output receives accountable human review
limitations: No prompting technique eliminates hallucinations
Risk varies with task, model, retrieval, and review quality
editorialIntro: A hallucination is when AI states something false with complete confidence. It is built into how these systems work, so your job is to manage it, not wish it away.

blocks.text: A hallucination is AI output that is fluent, confident, and false: invented facts, fake citations, made-up quotes, nonexistent people, or plausible numbers with no basis. The unsettling part is the confidence. The model shows no doubt when it invents, because it does not know it is inventing. It is doing what it always does, predicting likely text, and sometimes the most likely-sounding text is simply not true.
Why they happen

A language model generates each word by predicting what should come next from patterns, not by looking up a stored fact and confirming it. When it has seen a fact many times in training, its prediction usually matches reality. When it has not, or when your question sits in a gap, it still produces a confident, well-formed answer because that is what it was built to do. It fills the gap with something shaped like a correct answer. A fake legal citation looks exactly like a real one because the model learned the pattern of citations, not the case law. That is the mechanism, and it is why hallucinations can only be managed, never fully removed.
Who this is for

items: Anyone who relies on AI for facts, citations, or numbers.
Owners and managers writing AI-use policy and setting review requirements.
Professionals in high-stakes fields where a false statement carries liability.

blocks.text: When to use it

Keep this front of mind whenever AI output will be treated as fact: research, citations, compliance statements, medical or legal or financial content, and anything a customer, court, or regulator will read. The riskier the setting, the more this lesson applies. Share it with your team before anyone uses AI on client-facing work.
When not to worry

Purely generative tasks with no factual claim need no hallucination guard: rewording your own text, brainstorming names, drafting a tone for an email you will fact-check anyway. If there is no claim about the world, there is nothing to hallucinate. Concentrate your attention where facts live, and let AI do the creative and drafting work it handles well.
No tool eliminates hallucinations, but some lower the rate or bring inventions into the open.
Source-citing tools
Perplexity and search-enabled chat give you links to check and lower the rate of pure invention. Still open and verify each link.
Retrieval-grounded assistants
Answering only from your own documents constrains the model to supplied text, which cuts invention when the system is built well.
Confidence-flagging prompts
Ask the model to rate its own certainty and name exactly what you should check before trusting the answer.
The primary source itself
The only real fix: confirm the fact where it actually lives, in the case record, the report, or the original data.

items: Assume any specific fact could be invented until confirmed, especially names, citations, statistics, and quotes.
Prefer grounded modes. Use tools that cite sources or answer from your own documents when facts matter.
Ask for sources and confidence, then treat low-confidence items as unverified by default.
Check every citation twice: does it exist, and does it say what was claimed?
Never submit AI-generated citations or figures to a court, client, or regulator without independent confirmation.
Build a review gate so no unverified claim reaches anyone outside your team.

blocks.text: Answer only from the document I pasted. If the document does not contain the answer, say "not in the source" rather than filling it in from general knowledge.

List every citation, statistic, name, and date in your answer. For each, tell me your confidence it is real and correct, and exactly where I should go to verify it. Flag anything you may have invented.

editorialSections.title: What happened in Mata v. Avianca

blocks.text: The clearest cautionary tale is Mata v. Avianca. In 2023, in the U. S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, lawyers filed a brief citing several court decisions to support their client's case. The problem: the cases did not exist. The attorneys had used ChatGPT for legal research, and the tool had hallucinated six judicial opinions, complete with case names, citations, quotations, and reasoning that read like the real thing. When opposing counsel and the court could not find the cases, the lawyers asked ChatGPT to confirm them, and the tool insisted they were real and could be found on Westlaw and LexisNexis. They were not.

Judge P. Kevin Castel sanctioned the attorneys under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11, imposing a $5,000 penalty and requiring them to notify each judge who had been falsely named as the author of a fabricated opinion. The case became a global warning and is now routinely cited when AI-invented case law appears in court. In 2024 the American Bar Association issued its first formal ethics opinion on lawyers' use of generative AI.

The takeaway is not that AI is dangerous and should be avoided. The lawyers skipped the one step that would have caught everything: opening a legal database and confirming the cases existed. The tool did what tools do. The humans did not verify.
Submitting AI citations without checking
The Mata mistake. Fake citations look identical to real ones, so a quick glance never catches them. Open the source every time.
Asking the model to confirm itself
It will often double down on the invention with more confidence. Confirmation has to come from outside the model.
Assuming newer or bigger models do not hallucinate
They hallucinate less, not never. The verification habit still applies at every model size.
Trusting a cited link without opening it
Models sometimes attach a real URL to a claim the page does not actually make. Read the page, not just the link.
No review gate
Without a required check before publication, one confident invention can reach a customer or a court.

items: Did I confirm every citation both exists and supports the claim?
Did I verify every name, statistic, quote, and date against a primary source?
Did I avoid using the same model to confirm its own claims?
For grounded tasks, did the answer stay inside the supplied documents?
Is there a required review gate before anything factual reaches an outside party?
For legal, medical, or financial content, did a qualified professional sign off?

title: How to verify AI outputs
summary: A repeatable method for checking AI answers against primary sources and guarding against the false trust created by fluent output.
audience: Anyone who must decide whether an AI-generated claim is accurate enough to use.
evidence: Primary sources for each material claim
methodology: Extract discrete factual claims
Rank claims by consequence
Locate the controlling or primary source
Compare the exact claim with the source
Correct, qualify, or remove unsupported language
Preserve citations and review notes
assumptions: Authoritative sources can be accessed
The reviewer understands the relevant domain or can escalate
limitations: Verification is bounded by source availability and reviewer competence
A source can exist without supporting the claim made
editorialIntro: A fast, repeatable way to check AI answers against primary sources, and why fluent output slips past your judgment so easily.

blocks.text: Verification is the deliberate step of confirming an AI claim against a trustworthy source before you act on it or pass it along. It is a discipline, not a feeling. It has to be a discipline because the natural human response to fluent, confident writing is to believe it, and AI produces fluent, confident writing by design.
Why fluent output lowers your guard

Your brain treats things that are easy to process as more likely to be true. Psychologists call this processing fluency, and it is well documented: text that reads smoothly, in a clean font, in a confident voice, feels more credible than the same claim delivered awkwardly. AI output is tuned to be maximally fluent. It is grammatical, organized, and self-assured, so it presses the exact button that lowers your guard. You are not gullible for trusting it. You are human, and the output is tuned to that humanity. The fix is to move the trust decision out of your gut and into a checklist you run every time. That is what the rest of this lesson gives you.

items: Anyone publishing, sending, or deciding based on AI output.
Teams setting a standard so verification does not depend on who happens to be careful that day.
Professionals in fields where a wrong fact carries real consequences.

blocks.text: Verify before anything factual leaves your hands: a claim a customer will read, a number in a proposal, a name or quote attributed to a real person, a citation, a legal or regulatory statement, a statistic. The trigger is simple. If it is a fact and being wrong would cost something, verify it. The higher the stakes, the more independent your source needs to be.

You do not need to verify subjective or generative work where no external fact exists to check: the tone of a draft email, brainstormed slogan options, a rewrite of your own paragraph. If the output makes no claim about the world, there is nothing to verify, only quality to judge. Spending verification effort on taste questions wastes the effort and dulls the habit for the claims that need it. Reserve verification for facts.

cells.text: A law, regulation, or government rule
The official government site (.gov), the actual statute or agency page
Google Scholar, the original study, the primary data source
The original speech, article, or a reputable outlet reporting it
A product spec, price, or policy
A spreadsheet or calculator; redo it yourself

blocks.text: Tools that cite sources (Perplexity, search-enabled chat) speed the first step by handing you a link. They do not finish the job. You still open the link and confirm it says what the tool claims, because models sometimes cite a real page that does not actually support the statement.
Run this every time before a factual output leaves your hands.

items: ✓ Did I list every checkable claim, not just the ones that jumped out?
✓ Did I go to a primary source rather than another AI or a secondhand summary?
✓ For each citation, did I confirm both that it exists and that it supports the claim?
✓ Did I redo any math myself?
✓ Did I flag, not bury, anything I could not verify?
✓ Did I resist the pull to trust it just because it read well?
Separate facts from framing. Underline every checkable claim: names, numbers, dates, citations, quotes, rules.
Rank by stakes. Which of these, if wrong, actually hurt? Check those hardest.
Go to the primary source, not another summary. The government page, the study, the original document.
Confirm the source exists and says it. For citations, this is two checks: does the source exist, and does it support the claim?
Redo any math yourself. Do not trust arithmetic done in the model's head.
Note what you could not verify. Flag it clearly rather than letting an unverified claim ride along as if confirmed.
Only then act, send, or publish.

blocks.text: Enlist the model in its own verification. Its answer is a starting point, not proof.

For every factual claim, citation, statistic, and proper name in your previous answer, add a bracketed confidence note: [high], [medium], or [low], and say what a human should check to confirm it. Do not soften low-confidence items.
You cited a source. Quote the exact sentence from that source that supports the claim. If you cannot quote it, say so plainly and tell me the claim is unverified.
This surfaces the shaky parts fast. It does not replace opening the source yourself.

editorialSections.title: What a good self-audit looks like

blocks.text: Asked to self-audit, a well-behaved model flags its own weak points:

"The three-year retention rule [high, from federal labor regulations, confirm on dol.gov]. The claim that penalties start at $1,100 per violation [low, I'm not confident in this exact figure, verify on the agency's penalty schedule]. The 2019 date I gave [medium, check the agency's amendment history]."

That output does not end your work. It tells you where to point it. You open dol.gov, confirm the retention rule, and either fix or delete the penalty figure the model flagged as low confidence. The unverified number never reaches your customer.
Trusting fluency
The core trap. Smooth prose feels true, and that feeling is not evidence.
Verifying with the same tool that made the claim
Asking the model "are you sure?" often just yields a new confident answer. Go outside the model.
Accepting a citation without opening it
A link is not a fact-check. The page may not say what the tool claims, or may not exist.
Checking a summary against another summary
Go to the primary source, or you are just comparing two guesses.
Verifying only the obvious claims
The dangerous errors are the plausible ones you did not think to question.

title: Privacy and confidentiality basics
summary: What is safe to enter into an AI tool, what is not, and how consumer, business, and enterprise controls can differ for training, retention, and access.
audience: Professionals and teams handling client, employee, patient, student, customer, or proprietary information.
evidence: Current vendor terms and privacy documentation
Applicable professional, contractual, and regulatory duties
methodology: Classify the information before entry
Check authority and purpose
Verify vendor tier, training, retention, and access controls
Minimize or de-identify data
Use an approved alternative when requirements are unmet
assumptions: Organizations can identify data owners and applicable policies
Vendor settings and terms are checked at the time of use
limitations: Vendor practices and product controls change
This lesson does not replace legal, privacy, security, or professional advice
editorialIntro: Before you paste one more thing into a chat box: here is what the tool keeps, who can see it, and the real gap between a free login and a business contract.

editorialSections.title: A working rule for what goes in the chat box

blocks.text: Every time you paste text into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Copilot, it leaves your computer and lands on a vendor's servers. Three questions decide whether that is fine or a problem.

Is it stored? For how long? And can it be used to train a future model that other people will use? The answers depend almost entirely on which tier you are on. A personal free login and a paid business plan from the same company can handle your data in completely different ways.
Most people never learn that difference. That is how confidential client details end up in a system nobody at the company controls.
Vendor policies described here were checked in mid-2026. Data terms change often, so treat this as a starting map. Confirm each vendor's current policy at the source before you rely on it.

editorialSections.title: People who handle other people's data

items: Owners and managers about to let a team use AI tools, who want one clear rule instead of a vague worry.
Anyone in a regulated or contract-bound field: healthcare, law, finance, education, or any business that signed confidentiality terms with clients.
Solo operators who handle client lists, health details, or financials and want to keep using AI without breaking a promise they made.

editorialSections.title: Run this thinking before anything non-public

items: Before you draft your team's AI usage rule or hand anyone a login.
Before pasting a customer record, contract, medical note, financial statement, résumé, or anything with a name attached to a fact.
When choosing between a free tool and a paid business tier, so privacy terms drive the decision instead of price.

editorialSections.title: What this lesson does not replace
editorialSections.eyebrow: When NOT to rely on it alone

blocks.text: This gives you a sensible default. It does not stand in for these.
A signed contract
If your client agreement, HIPAA obligations, or a data processing agreement forbid sending data to third parties, this lesson does not override that. Read the contract.
Legal review of vendor terms
Nothing here is legal advice. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. For anything high-stakes, have a qualified lawyer read the vendor's data terms and your own obligations.
The assumption that a paid plan is a vault
Paid tiers reduce risk; they do not make a tool private by default. Human reviewers can still see flagged content, and misconfigured settings are common.

The pattern is consistent: consumer plans may use your chats to improve models unless you opt out, while business and enterprise plans do not train on your data by default. Retention also drops as you move up.
Simplified comparison, verified mid-2026. Always re-check current terms at each vendor's own privacy page.

cells.text: Trains on your content by default?
Yes, unless you opt out in Data Controls
Kept until you delete; deleted chats purged within ~30 days. A copy of temporary chats is held ~30 days for abuse monitoring.
Admin controls retention; deleted conversations removed within ~30 days.
Only if you leave "Improve Claude for everyone" on; opted-in chats can be retained up to 5 years. Off returns you to 30-day retention with no training.
30 days when training is off; up to 5 years when on.
No. API standard log retention is ~7 days. Zero Data Retention available for qualifying Enterprise customers.
~7 days (API) to as low as zero (ZDR).
No. Content stays in your tenant and is not used to train the underlying models.
Governed by your Microsoft 365 tenant policies.
No. Workspace data is not used to train models outside your organization.
Governed by your Workspace admin policies.

blocks.text: One nuance to know: even when a vendor says it does not train on your data, most reserve the right to have a human review content flagged for safety or abuse. Anthropic's mid-2026 policy is explicit that conversations flagged for safety review can be used in ways that override a stated training preference, and it does not spell out what triggers a flag. Treat "not used for training" as strong protection, not an absolute guarantee of secrecy.

editorialSections.title: Sort, set the rule, then paste

items: Sort your data into three buckets. Green: already public, no identifiable person or secret. Yellow: internal but not sensitive (draft copy, generic process notes). Red: any real name tied to health, money, legal status, or a promise of confidentiality.
Set the rule. Green goes anywhere. Yellow goes only into a business or enterprise tier with training off. Red does not go in at all unless a contract and configuration specifically permit it.
Strip before you paste. For yellow items, remove names and identifiers first. "Client A, a 54-year-old" carries far less risk than a real name.
Check the account settings once, in writing. Confirm the tier, the training toggle, and the retention setting. Screenshot it. Settings get changed and reset.
Turn off training and history where you can. On consumer tiers, use data controls and temporary or incognito modes for anything you would not want retained.
Write it down for the team. A one-page rule everyone can follow beats a perfect policy nobody reads.

blocks.text: Use these to have the tool help build your own policy. None of them contain real confidential data.

You are helping a small business write a plain-language AI usage rule. Our team uses [ChatGPT Business / Gemini in Workspace]. Draft a one-page policy covering: what data is never allowed in AI tools, what must be anonymized first, which tier and settings are required, and who to ask when unsure. Keep it under 300 words and write it for non-technical staff.

I'm about to paste the text below into an AI tool. Before I do, tell me: does it contain any personal identifiers, health, financial, or legal details that would make it risky to send to a third party? List anything I should remove or mask first. Do not store or repeat the content back. [paste ONLY non-confidential sample text here to test the process]

Rewrite this internal note so it keeps the useful structure but removes every name, account number, and detail that could identify a real person or client. Replace them with generic placeholders like [Client A].

editorialSections.title: What the policy prompt might return

blocks.text: AI Usage Rule — [Company]

items: Never paste into any AI tool: client names tied to health or financial details, Social Security or account numbers, passwords, signed contracts, or anything covered by a confidentiality agreement.
Internal drafts and generic notes are allowed only in our approved Business plan, with model training turned off.
Before pasting anything about a specific person, replace their name with a placeholder.
When unsure, ask [name] before pasting. A five-minute question beats a data leak.

blocks.text: Realistic, but the model may invent settings names or overstate a protection. That is exactly why the review step exists.
Assuming free equals private
On most consumer tiers, your chats can train the next model unless you opt out. This is the single most common mistake.
Pasting client data to save five minutes
A confidentiality breach is not undone by deleting the chat afterward.
Trusting a browser extension or unknown app
Third-party wrappers may route your text through servers with no clear policy. Prefer the vendor's own app.
Letting the model describe its own privacy terms
Models frequently get their own vendor's policy wrong. Verify at the source, not by asking the chatbot.
Setting the policy once and forgetting it
Vendors update terms and defaults reset. Re-check quarterly.

items: I confirmed which tier we are actually on, not the one we think we bought.
I verified the training and retention settings at the vendor's own page, today.
No red-bucket data (names tied to health, money, legal status, or a confidentiality promise) is in this prompt.

editorialIntro: You don't need ten subscriptions. You need one assistant, one tool that already lives where you work, and maybe one specialist. Here's how to pick, without the hype.

blocks.text: A method for assembling a small, deliberate set of AI tools that fits a small business, instead of collecting subscriptions because a newsletter told you to.

A good starter stack has three slots at most: a general assistant for thinking and drafting, a tool built into the software you already use, and possibly one specialist for a job the first two do poorly. That's the whole thing. Restraint here saves money and, more importantly, saves the attention it takes to actually get good at a tool.

items: Owners of small businesses and solo operators making their first real AI purchase.
Teams already paying for three or four AI tools nobody has learned, who want to cut back to what earns its keep.
Anyone stuck on the number of options who wants a decision rule, not a 40-tool comparison spreadsheet.
You're about to spend money on AI and want the decision to be intentional.
You already run one tool well and are wondering whether to add a second.
Your team's tools have crept upward and you want to prune to a stack you can defend.

blocks.text: Three moments where building a stack works against you.
Before you have a real task
Don't build a stack in the abstract. Pick one recurring job that eats your time, then choose a tool for it. Tools chosen without a task go unused.
When your data rules aren't settled
If you handle regulated or confidential data, decide your privacy and tier requirements first. A cheap consumer tool that violates a client agreement is not a bargain.
When you're chasing the newest release
Switching stacks every time a model tops a benchmark burns the time you should spend getting fluent. For a first stack, stability beats novelty.
Match a tool to each slot. You won't fill all three on day one, and that's fine.
Pricing and plan names below were checked mid-2026 and shift often. Confirm current numbers on each vendor's site before you buy.

cells.text: Drafting, brainstorming, summarizing, thinking out loud
ChatGPT (Free, Plus ~$20/mo, or Business), Claude (Free or paid), Gemini
AI inside the email, docs, and files you already use
Microsoft 365 Copilot (add-on, ~$30/user/mo) if you're on Microsoft; Gemini in Google Workspace if you're on Google

blocks.text: The biggest lever most people miss: if you already pay for Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, your workspace-native slot is often the highest-value add. It works on your real documents and, at the paid business tier, doesn't train on your data by default. Start there before buying a fourth standalone tool.

items: List your top three time-eaters. The recurring tasks that drain hours: email, proposals, notes, research, scheduling.
Pick the one worth automating first. Highest frequency times highest annoyance wins.
Set your data floor. Decide the minimum tier and privacy setting that task requires. Regulated data raises the floor.
Fill the general-assistant slot. Try two free tiers on the same real task for a week. Keep the one whose output you trust and whose interface you enjoy.
Check your workspace-native option. If you're already on Microsoft or Google, test their built-in AI on your actual files before buying anything else.
Add a specialist only if a real gap remains. No gap, no purchase.
Set a 30-day review. If a tool isn't used weekly, cancel it.

blocks.text: Use a general assistant to pressure-test your own choices.

I run a [type] business with [N] people. We use [Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace]. Our three biggest time-drains are [A], [B], [C]. Recommend a lean AI stack of no more than three tools, explain what each is FOR, and tell me which ONE to start with this week. Flag anything I'd be paying for twice.

Compare [Tool A] and [Tool B] for this exact task: [describe task]. Give me a short table of the tradeoffs that actually matter for a small business, not a feature dump. End with a one-line recommendation and the main risk of that choice.
Here's my current list of AI subscriptions and what I use each for: [list]. Which are redundant? What could I cancel without losing a capability I actually rely on?
For a 4-person services firm on Google Workspace:

items: Start here: Gemini in Google Workspace. It already sits in your Gmail and Docs, and at your paid tier it won't train on your data. Use it for email drafts and document cleanup.
General assistant: One of Claude or ChatGPT, paid tier, for brainstorming and longer drafting where you want a separate scratchpad.
Specialist: Hold off. Add a meeting-notes tool only if you run enough calls to justify it.
Skip for now: A second general assistant. Two do the same job; pick one and get fluent.

blocks.text: Treat any specific price or plan name a model gives you as a claim to verify. Models routinely state outdated pricing.
Buying breadth instead of depth
Three well-used tools beat eight half-learned ones. Depth is where the payoff lives.
Paying twice for the same capability
Your workspace suite may already include what you're about to buy separately. Check before you subscribe.
Ignoring the data tier to save $10
The cheap plan may train on your inputs or violate a client agreement. The savings aren't worth the exposure.
Chasing benchmarks
The model that won this month's leaderboard is rarely worth re-training your team on.
No cancel-by date
Unused subscriptions renew silently. Set a review and hold the line.

items: Each tool maps to a specific recurring task, not a vague hope.
I confirmed I'm not paying twice for a capability already in my suite.
The tier and privacy settings meet my data obligations.

editorialIntro: Turn a messy call into clean decisions and next steps in minutes. First, get the consent part right, because that is where this goes wrong.

blocks.text: The consent laws described here are general and were checked mid-2026. They are not legal advice, and recording rules vary by state and country. Confirm your obligations with a qualified attorney.

A workflow for using AI to capture meetings and produce a useful record: a short summary, the decisions made, and a clear list of who owes what by when. AI notetakers transcribe a call and draft this automatically. The transcription and summary are the easy, valuable part. The part people skip, and the part that has produced real lawsuits, is telling everyone in the room that a bot is recording and getting their agreement first.

items: Anyone who runs client calls, team meetings, or interviews and wants a reliable record without typing through the conversation.
Small teams that lose decisions and action items because notes were an afterthought.
Owners who want the productivity of an AI notetaker without stepping on privacy law.
Recurring internal meetings where you keep re-litigating what was decided.
Client or project calls where the follow-up list is the whole point.
Long calls you'd otherwise transcribe by hand.
Any meeting where everyone present knows and agrees to the recording.

blocks.text: The core rule: notice is not consent. Give people a genuine way to say no before recording begins, and honor it. When in doubt, ask a qualified attorney about your jurisdiction.
You haven't gotten consent

Eleven US states require all-party consent to record a conversation: California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Montana, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Washington. A vague "this meeting may be recorded" line in a calendar invite is not affirmative consent and may not satisfy the law. Everyone needs a real chance to decline before recording starts.
Privileged or highly sensitive conversations
Legal strategy, HR investigations, medical discussions, board deliberations: an automatic transcript can waive privilege or create discoverable records. Keep the bot out.
Confidential third-party data going to an unvetted tool

Several popular notetakers send audio to their own servers and have faced biometric-privacy suits over voiceprints. Don't route confidential data through a tool whose data handling you haven't checked.
As a substitute for being present
A transcript is not attention. Don't skip meetings because a bot is there.
Two broad families, with different privacy profiles. Verify each vendor's current data terms before adopting.

items: Platform-native capture keeps audio inside the meeting platform you already trust. Zoom's AI Companion, Microsoft Teams (with Copilot), and Google Meet transcribe and summarize without a third-party bot joining. This is usually the lower-risk starting point, especially on paid business tiers that don't train on your content.

Standalone notetakers such as Otter, Fireflies, Fathom, and Read AI join as a participant and record to their own servers. They're capable, but you're adding a vendor, and some have faced consent and biometric-privacy litigation. Vet the data policy and consent mechanism before you use one on client calls.

Manual capture plus a general assistant: take your own rough notes, then paste them (de-identified) into Claude or ChatGPT to structure decisions and action items. No recording, no consent issue, still a big time save.
Decide if recording is even needed. Structured notes from your own rough capture are often enough, and skip the consent problem entirely.
Get consent, out loud, before recording. "I'd like to use an AI notetaker for this call so we have accurate notes. Any objection?" Wait for a real answer. Don't start until you have it.
Prefer platform-native capture where you can, to avoid adding a vendor.
Let it transcribe and draft. Get the raw transcript or auto-summary.
Restructure into a usable record. Summary, decisions, and an owner-plus-due-date action list. Use the prompt below.
Verify against reality. Fix misheard names, wrong numbers, and any action item the model invented or garbled.
Send the recap promptly so attendees can correct it while memories are fresh.

blocks.text: Here is a meeting transcript. Produce: 1. A 4-bullet summary of what the meeting was about. 2. DECISIONS: every decision that was actually made (not just discussed). 3. ACTION ITEMS: a table of task, owner, and due date. If a due date wasn't stated, write "not set" rather than guessing. Flag anything ambiguous where you're inferring rather than quoting. [paste transcript — remove sensitive details first]

From these rough notes I typed during a call, write a clean recap email to attendees: a short intro line, the decisions we reached, and a who-owes-what list. Keep it under 200 words and neutral in tone. [paste your notes]
Review this action-item list against the transcript. Did you attribute any task to the wrong person, or invent a deadline that was never said? Correct it and show me what you changed.
Decisions

items: Ship the pricing page update this week; hold the blog post until legal reviews the claims.
Move the standing sync from Monday to Wednesday.

blocks.text: Action items

items: Draft revised pricing copy — Owner: Priya — Due: Thu
Send claims to legal — Owner: Marcus — Due: not set
Update the calendar invite — Owner: Priya — Due: today

blocks.text: What to catch: notetakers mishear names ("Priya" vs "Prea"), attach the wrong owner to a task, and sometimes list a discussed idea as a decision. The verify step is not optional; it's where the record becomes trustworthy.
Recording without real consent
The most serious risk, and the source of actual lawsuits.
Letting a bot into privileged meetings
Can waive privilege or create discoverable records.
Trusting the summary as-is
Misheard names and invented action items go out under your name.
Adopting a standalone tool without vetting its data policy
Some store audio and voiceprints on their servers.
Over-recording
Not every meeting needs a permanent transcript; some are better off without one.

title: AI for SOP drafting
summary: A workflow for turning a process that lives in someone's head into a documented standard operating procedure, with human review that keeps it accurate and safe to follow.
audience: Operators, founders, and teams documenting repeatable internal processes.
evidence: Representative inputs, outputs, exceptions, and failure cases
Policies and systems governing the process
methodology: Observe or interview the process owner
Map triggers, inputs, steps, decisions, and handoffs
Draft in a standard structure
Test the procedure with a different user
Correct omissions and unsafe assumptions
Assign an owner and review date
assumptions: A knowledgeable process owner validates the procedure
The process can be tested before broad adoption
limitations: AI cannot discover tacit steps that users fail to provide
Regulated, safety-critical, or high-consequence procedures require qualified review and change control
